title.en: Bob Dylan and a new generation of songwriters
title.zh: Bob Dylan，美国新一代歌曲创作者

summary.en: Bob Dylan begins as a folk performer, widens what a traditional folk singer can do, and helps open the singer-songwriter model.
summary.zh: Bob Dylan从一开始的folk performer（民谣表演者），逐渐拓宽了传统民谣歌手的思维方式，开创了singer-songwriter（歌手-创作人）模式。

body.zh:
Bob Dylan从一开始的folk performer（民谣表演者），逐渐拓宽了传统民谣歌手的思维方式，开创了singer-songwriter（歌手-创作人）模式。

欢迎来到摇滚史第五章，这一章我们说说美国对于英伦入侵的回应。先复习一下讲过的内容，我们已经讲过1955到1959年，摇滚乐的第一波浪潮，像Elvis、Buddy Holly、Chuck Berry和Fats Domino等人，他们的影响力随着1950年代的结束而渐渐消却。Buddy Holly乘坐的飞机在1959年2月坠毁，人们说这是音乐死去的一天。然后我们讲到50年代末到1964年The Beatles登陆这段时期，还提出一个问题 ，从Elvis到The Beatles之间的这段时间，是流行音乐的黄金时代还是黑暗时代？1964年2月，The Beatles来了，伴随着英伦入侵的兴起，人们的印象是他们深刻地改变了摇滚乐，尤其是改变了美国的音乐市场。因为1960到63年那段时间，大家都在发掘下一个Elvis。结果从60到63年他们做的事没有一件和未来的Elvis沾得上边，下一个Elvis居然是The Beatles。The Beatles来自英格兰，他们是第一支用自己的方式成功打入美国市场的英国乐队。从各种角度来说，至今为止摇滚史上的两个大人物就是Elvis和The Beatles。英伦入侵并不像许多历史学家或是音乐记者所说的那样——严重的打乱了美国乐坛，但确实带来了不少变化。很多美国音乐人都感觉到，这些英国音乐人确实抢走了一部分生意。所以本章的内容就是，美国乐坛在63、64到67、68年这段时间做出的反应。

我们从一位重要人物说起，有人说他是60年代最重要的美国历史人物，那就是Bob Dylan。他的重要之处在于为流行音乐界的创作人树立了新的标杆。这之前我们的榜样是Brill Building（布里尔大厦）那种创作模式，他们是专业的写歌人，用的几乎都是匠人的方法。然后说到The Beatles，他们如何将63、64年的匠人模式变得更像是艺术创作。比如1966年的《Tomorrow Never Knows》和1967年早期的《Strawberry Fields Forever》、《Penny Lane》。这时工匠模式真正开始向艺术家模式转变，Dylan也在这波浪潮的中。The Beatles和Dylan之间也有许多互动，很多方面他们互相影响。

60年代初Dylan在纽约的格林威治村开始了他的职业生涯。如我此前所说，作为歌手，他直到1965年才有了第一首热门金曲。Dylan最初的几张专辑只被那些理解最纯粹民谣运动的人所知晓，连民谣复兴的人都不了解他的作品。民谣复兴指的是Peter, Paul and Mary、Kingston Trio、New Christy Minstrels这些组合，而不是像Bob Dylan这样的人，甚至Joan Baez也不算。Dylan在明尼苏达州的Duluth出生，在Hibbing长大。他的原名叫Robert Allen Zimmerman，之后改名为Bob Dylan，名字中的Dylan是受到了诗人Dylan Thomas的影响。1959年他进入明尼苏达大学，最初对摇滚乐感兴趣。1955到57年间的孩子们都会听Chuck Berry，然后是Buddy Holly和Elvis，所以Dylan当时就在不同的乐队里弹吉他和钢琴。

然而随着民谣复兴的兴起，Dylan对民谣的兴趣日益增长。受到Woody Guthrie的很大影响，他将自己塑造成了一名民谣歌手，开始在明尼苏达大学及当地进行民谣巡回演出。最终他搬到了纽约的格林威治村，开始了真正的音乐生涯。他的早期形象基于Woody Guthrie。Woody Guthrie那时被亨廷顿病 (Huntington's Disease) 缠身住在医院，据说Dylan常去探望。民谣界传言，Woody Guthrie可以说是将衣钵传给了Bob Dylan，某种程度上Dylan成了当时民谣运动的一颗新星。Dylan来到格林威治村，开始在不同俱乐部演出，他观察其他更有经验的人，并模仿他们。有趣的是，（现在的人可能不太会这么想）在Dylan早期的职业生涯中，他经常在表演中加入喜剧元素来赢得观众的喜爱，算是种冷幽默，并不下流。但是他身上有一些在众人面前扮小丑、出洋相的能力。我们愿意把Bob Dylan想象成极端认真或是带一点讽刺的人，但此时的他确实在试图交流，马上讲到的他在当时的一些作品就能看出。

总之Dylan在纽约给人留下了非常好的印象，他通过一个叫John Hammond的小伙子跟Columbia Records在1961年的秋天签约。要知道当时还没人知道Bob Dylan会成为怎样的人。1962年3月，他发行了第一张专辑《Bob Dylan》，销量惨淡。有报道说这张专辑第一年只卖出了五千张，这可是Bob Dylan啊。签下Bob Dylan被称作“Hammond的蠢事”，和Bob Dylan签约似乎是个大错误。之后Bob Dylan在1962年8月跟Albert Grossman签约，这个Grossman很懂如何经营Bob Dylan的职业生涯。不像50年代中期签约Elvis的Colonel Tom Parker那样，他做的事情是帮助Dylan重塑自我、重塑他的语言、他的形象和媒体宣传。Albert Grossman和John Hammond之间有过摩擦，所以Hammond不再担任Dylan的制作人。另一个叫做Tom Wilson的人出现了，这看上去只是一个小事，一般不会提及，但Tom Wilson担任Dylan的制作人在整个故事发展中十分重要，不只是对Dylan的早期专辑。1963年5月，Tom Wilson制作了他的第二张专辑 《The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan》，Dylan再次在民谣圈中获得认可，但没有很出名。他更多地作为一个创作者被人们熟知。1963年夏天，他的《Blowin' in the Wind》成为了Peter, Paul and Mary的热门金曲。他也录制了自己的版本，他的版本也许今天更流行、被更多人所熟知，但那个时候却被认为不适合在电台播放。Dylan的声音听起来没那么专业或受过训练，歌中伴奏的口琴旋律也没有按照专业标准进行雕琢，所以声音更加圆润悦耳的Peter, Paul and Mary版本成了热门单曲。专辑《The Times They Are A-Changin'》于1964年的1月问世，《Another Side Of Bob Dylan》于同年8月发行。以上都不是Bob Dylan的热门专辑，他并没有因此成为一名演艺明星，这些专辑更像是他的曲目表。

我们在讲1960到1963年那段时说过，相比青少年偶像和女子组合，民谣歌手更关注严肃的话题。作为民谣表演者（performer），Dylan遵循这种传统，表演了很多传统民谣歌曲，这些歌曲可以追溯到19世纪甚至更早，关注社会的平等、公正等话题。他也继续向歌曲创作者（songwriter）的方向发展，写自己的歌，发展自己的语言风格；而传统的观念是为大众创作，成为传统的一份子，为传统民谣增添新意义。这两者的冲突越来越明显。当时有评论说，Dylan不仅是一个歌曲创作者，而且他拓宽了传统民谣歌手的思维方式，他将传统民谣中的“我们”变成了“我”。这种思维，开创了一种singer-songwriter（歌手-创作人）模式，很多后人追随他的脚步。

想想早期的作品，《Blowin' in the Wind》是关于社会和政治主题的。也有布鲁斯风格的滑稽作品，《Motorpsycho Nitemare》就是极好的例子。也有浪漫的爱情歌曲，比如《Girl From The North Country》。如果你真的想听一首奠定了singer-songwriter标准的歌曲，我推荐《Don't Think Twice, It's All Right》。这首伟大的歌曲展示了Dylan的创作技巧，并且成为了人们心目中singer-songwriter作品的样本。《Don't Think Twice, It's All Right》和《Blowin' in the Wind》两首作品的主题完全不同，《Blowin' in the Wind》讲的是社会变革和公平公正，而《Don't Think Twice, It's All Right》说的是和女友的关系出现问题。这种从民谣到歌手-创作人的转变，是Dylan的一项重要贡献。在下节课中，我们会深入探讨Folk Rock（民谣摇滚）是如何诞生的，以及Dylan在直到1965年夏天这段时间的改变。他变得更像一个singer-songwriter，并在音乐中加入电声乐器，被视作美国乐坛回应英伦入侵的重要组成。
body.en:
Bob Dylan begins as a folk performer, widens what a traditional folk singer can do, and helps open the singer-songwriter model.

Welcome to Chapter 5 of the rock-history course—America’s reply to the British Invasion. Quick review: we covered 1955–1959, rock’s first wave—Elvis, Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, Fats Domino—whose pull fades as the 1950s end. Buddy Holly’s plane crashes in February 1959; people call it the day the music died. Then late 1950s to the Beatles’ 1964 landing: is the stretch from Elvis to the Beatles pop’s golden age or dark age? In February 1964 the Beatles arrive; with the Invasion, the impression is that they remake rock, especially the U.S. market. From 1960–63 everyone hunts the next Elvis. Nothing they try in those years points to the real next Elvis—who turns out to be the Beatles, from England, the first British band to break the U.S. market on their own terms. In many ways the two giants of rock history so far are Elvis and the Beatles. The Invasion does not wreck the American scene as hard as many historians and writers claim, but it does change things. Many U.S. musicians feel British acts take part of the business. This chapter is the American industry’s reply from about 1963–64 through 1967–68.

We start with someone some call the most important American figure of the 1960s: Bob Dylan. He matters because he sets a new bar for writers in pop. Before him the model is Brill Building—pro songwriters, mostly craft method. Then the Beatles: how they turn the 1963–64 craft model toward art—1966’s “Tomorrow Never Knows,” early 1967’s “Strawberry Fields Forever” and “Penny Lane.” Craft really starts shifting toward artist; Dylan is in that wave. The Beatles and Dylan interact and influence each other in many ways.

In the early 1960s Dylan starts his career in New York’s Greenwich Village. As I said, as a singer he has no hit of his own until 1965. His first albums are known mainly to people deepest in the pure folk scene—even folk-revival listeners often miss them. Folk revival here means Peter, Paul and Mary, the Kingston Trio, the New Christy Minstrels—not Dylan, and not even Joan Baez in that commercial sense. Dylan is born in Duluth, Minnesota, grows up in Hibbing. Born Robert Allen Zimmerman, he renames himself Bob Dylan after poet Dylan Thomas. In 1959 he enters the University of Minnesota, first interested in rock. Kids of 1955–57 hear Chuck Berry, then Buddy Holly and Elvis, so Dylan is already playing guitar and piano in bands.

As folk revival rises, his interest in folk grows. Strongly shaped by Woody Guthrie, he builds himself as a folk singer and tours folk around Minnesota. Eventually he moves to Greenwich Village and starts in earnest. Early image is based on Guthrie. Guthrie is then hospitalized with Huntington’s disease; Dylan is said to visit often. Folk lore has Guthrie passing the mantle to Dylan; in some sense Dylan becomes a new star of that movement. In the Village he plays clubs, watches more experienced players, copies them. Interestingly—modern listeners may not expect this—early Dylan often works comedy into the set: dry humor, not dirty, with a gift for clowning. We like to picture Dylan as stern or lightly ironic, but here he is trying to connect; some of the songs from this stretch show it.

Anyway he makes a strong New York impression and signs with Columbia through John Hammond in fall 1961. No one yet knows what Dylan will become. March 1962: debut album Bob Dylan—sales are poor. Reports say about five thousand copies the first year. Signing Dylan is called “Hammond’s folly”; it looks like a mistake. In August 1962 Dylan signs with Albert Grossman, who knows how to run the career—not Colonel Tom Parker’s mid-1950s Elvis model, but reshaping Dylan’s self, language, image, and press. Friction with Hammond ends Hammond’s producer role. Tom Wilson takes over—a detail often skipped, but Wilson as producer matters for the whole story, not only early Dylan LPs. May 1963: Wilson produces The Freewheelin’ Bob Dylan. Dylan is again respected in folk circles but not famous; he is better known as a writer. Summer 1963: “Blowin’ in the Wind” becomes a Peter, Paul and Mary hit. He records his own cut—today often better known—but then it is judged unfit for radio. Dylan’s voice sounds less trained; the harmonica is not polished to pro standards; the smoother PP&M version is the hit single. The Times They Are A-Changin’ arrives January 1964; Another Side of Bob Dylan that August. None are hit albums that make him a star; they read more like songbooks.

In our 1960–63 lectures we said folk singers, unlike teen idols and girl groups, lean toward serious subjects. As a folk performer Dylan follows that tradition—many traditional songs going back to the nineteenth century or earlier, about equality and justice. He also keeps moving as a songwriter, writing his own songs and voice; the older ideal is to write for the people, join tradition, add to it. The tension grows. Critics say Dylan is not only a songwriter: he widens the folk singer’s mindset, turning folk’s “we” into “I.” That opens a singer-songwriter model many later follow.

Early work: “Blowin’ in the Wind” is social and political. There are comic blues pieces—“Motorpsycho Nitemare” is a strong example—and romantic songs like “Girl from the North Country.” For a song that sets singer-songwriter standards, try “Don’t Think Twice, It’s All Right”: craft on display, and a template for the form. Its subject is nothing like “Blowin’ in the Wind”—social change and fairness there; here a relationship going wrong. That shift from folk performer toward singer-songwriter is a major Dylan contribution. Next lecture: how folk rock is born, and Dylan’s change through summer 1965—more singer-songwriter, electric instruments added—as a key piece of America’s reply to the Invasion.
